claims.text: Map projection transforms the three-dimensional surface of the Earth onto a two-dimensional plane.
claims.label: flattening the globe onto a plane

claims.text: A sphere cannot be flattened without altering its shape and proportions, so every projection involves distortion.
claims.label: the unavoidable distortion

claims.text: Each projection is a compromise: it deliberately distorts certain properties of the Earth in order to minimise distortion in others.
claims.label: the compromise every projection makes

claims.text: Projections prioritise different properties, such as area, shape, distance, or direction, so no single projection is correct for all purposes.
claims.label: the lack of one correct projection

claims.text: The Mercator projection preserves angles, which makes it useful for navigation, but it greatly exaggerates the size of landmasses near the poles, such as Greenland.
claims.label: the Mercator projection

claims.text: The Gall-Peters projection depicts the relative sizes of continents accurately but significantly distorts their shapes.
claims.label: the Gall-Peters projection

claims.text: Cylindrical projections wrap the Earth around a cylinder, while conic projections such as the Lambert Conformal Conic suit regions with irregular shapes like South America.
claims.label: cylindrical and conic projections
